title: Observational study
description: Study with uncontrolled variable of interest
wiki_lead:
An observational study is a type of research design in which outcomes are measured to identify patterns or associations without attempts by the investigator to manipulate variables or conditions.   
Observational studies are commonly used in fields such as medicine, epidemiology, psychology, sociology, and statistics.   
Observational studies are one of two types of clinical study design, which can be either experimental or observational. In an experimental study, particularly a randomized controlled trial (RTC), test subjects are randomly assigned to either a treatment group (who receive the intervention or treatment being studied, i.e. the independent variable) or a control group (who do not), and the researcher compares the outcomes of the two groups. By contrast, in an observational study, the researcher does not determine the assignment of subjects, and there may not be a control group; if there is a control group, assignment of the independent variable is not under the control of the researcher.  
Although such studies can be rigorously designed, due of the lack of a random assignment mechanism, observational studies naturally present difficulties for inferential analysis, are susceptible to confounding and bias, and produce a lower quality of evidence than RTCs. 
An observational study might be performed if an RCT is unethical, impractical, or outside the control of the investigator. Observational studies are often pragmatic, being designed to show real-world effectiveness without attempting to understand underlying mechanisms. Indeed, regardless of its quality, an observational study cannot, on its own, establish causality.
wiki_excerpt:
An observational study is a type of research design in which outcomes are measured to identify patterns or associations without attempts by the investigator to manipulate variables or conditions.   
Observational studies are commonly used in fields such as medicine, epidemiology, psychology, sociology, and statistics.   
Observational studies are one of two types of clinical study design, which can be either experimental or observational. In an experimental study, particularly a randomized controlled trial (RTC), test subjects are randomly assigned to either a treatment group (who receive the intervention or treatment being studied, i.e. the independent variable) or a control group (who do not), and the researcher compares the outcomes of the two groups. By contrast, in an observational study, the researcher does not determine the assignment of subjects, and there may not be a control group; if there is a control group, assignment of the independent variable is not under the control of the researcher.  
Although such studies can be rigorously designed, due of the lack of a random assignment mechanism, observational studies naturally present difficulties for inferential analysis, are susceptible to confounding and bias, and produce a lower quality of evidence than RTCs. 
An observational study might be performed if an RCT is unethical, impractical, or outside the control of the investigator. Observational studies are often pragmatic, being designed to show real-world effectiveness without attempting to understand underlying mechanisms. Indeed, regardless of its quality, an observational study cannot, on its own, establish causality.


Motivations
The independent variable may be beyond the control of the investigator for a variety of reasons, for instance: 

Conducting an RCT may violate ethical standards. For instance, in a hypothetical trial seeking to prove that smoking cigarettes causes lung cancer, it would be unethical to randomly assign a group of participants to smoke. (However, observational studies are not automatically free of ethical considerations, and, depending on the study design, may still put participants at risk of harm; for instance they may involve an invasive or high-risk means of collecting data from participants.)
The researcher may lack control over the situation.  Suppose a scientist wants to study the public health effects of a community-wide ban on smoking in public indoor areas.  In a controlled experiment, the investigator would randomly pick a set of communities to be in the treatment group.  However, it is typically up to each community and/or its legislature to enact a smoking ban.  The investigator can be expected to lack the political power to cause precisely those communities in the randomly selected treatment group to pass a smoking ban.  In an observational study, the investigator would typically start with a treatment group consisting of those communities where a smoking ban is already in effect.
A randomized experiment may be impractical.  Suppose a researcher wants to study the suspected link between a certain medication and a very rare group of symptoms arising as a side effect.  Setting aside any ethical considerations, a randomized experiment may not be practical due to rare outcomes.  There may not be a subject pool large enough for the symptoms to be observed in at least one treated subject.  An observational study would typically start with a group of symptomatic subjects and work backwards to find those who were given the medication and later developed the symptoms. So the treated group is identified based on symptoms, instead of by random assignment.
Many randomized controlled trials are not broadly representative of real-world patients and this may not reflect real-world conditions. Patients who are eligible for inclusion in a randomized controlled trial are usually younger, more likely to be male, healthier and more likely to be treated according to recommendations from guidelin
grok_lead: An observational study is a research design in which investigators observe and measure variables of interest among participants without assigning interventions, manipulations, or treatments to influence outcomes. These studies are widely used in epidemiology and other disciplines to examine associations between exposures (such as risk factors or behaviors) and health outcomes (like diseases) in natural, uncontrolled settings, allowing researchers to draw inferences about potential causation while respecting ethical constraints on experimentation. Unlike experimental studies, where exposures are deliberately controlledâsuch as in randomized clinical trialsâobservational approaches rely on existing variations in the population to identify patterns. Observational studies encompass several primary designs, each suited to different research questions and data availability. Cohort studies follow groups of individuals (cohorts) defined by exposure status over time to compare incidence rates of outcomes, enabling calculation of relative risks; prospective cohorts track participants forward from exposure, while retrospective ones analyze historical data. Notable examples include the Framingham Heart Study, which has monitored cardiovascular risk factors since the 1950s, and the Nurses' Health Study, following over 100,000 nurses to assess lifestyle impacts on disease. Case-control studies, conversely, start with individuals who have the outcome (cases) and compare their prior exposures to those without the outcome (controls), often using odds ratios to estimate associations; this design proved pivotal in linking contaminated salsa to a 2003 hepatitis A outbreak, where 94% of cases reported consumption versus 39% of controls. Cross-sectional studies provide a snapshot by measuring exposures and outcomes simultaneously in a population at a single point, ideal for estimating prevalence but limited in establishing temporality. These studies offer distinct advantages, particularly for investigating rare events, long-term effects, or ethically sensitive exposures that cannot be tested experimentally, such as the harms of smoking or environmental toxins. They are often more cost-effective and feasible for large-scale, real-world applications, providing evidence on drug safety and effectiveness in pharmacoepidemiology, as seen in analyses of diabetes treatments using administrative databases. However, observational designs are prone to biases, including confounding (where unmeasured factors influence both exposure and outcome), selection bias, and information bias, which can distort associations and necessitate advanced statistical adjustments like propensity score matching. Despite these limitations, rigorous reporting guidelines such as STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) and the more recent TARGET 2025 guideline help enhance transparency and validity, making observational evidence a cornerstone for public health policy and clinical guidelines when randomized trials are impractical.
